summary: Defines the addressing architecture of IP version 6, including how addresses are written, the types of addresses, and how they are used. It was replaced by RFC 3513.

plainLanguage.summary: The rulebook for the newer, much longer internet addresses and the different kinds they come in.

questions: what is the ipv6 loopback address
subtitle: How 128-bit IPv6 addresses are written, divided into types, and which ones every node must recognize.

tldr.problem: IPv6 needed a defined addressing model: how addresses look, what kinds exist, and how they are written and assigned.
tldr.mechanism: Addresses are 128-bit identifiers for interfaces, of three types (unicast, anycast, multicast), with no broadcast. The leading bits (the Format Prefix) indicate the type, and the RFC defines text forms, special addresses and the addresses each node must know.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2373 obsoleted RFC 1884 and has itself been obsoleted by RFC 3513.

today: RFC 2373 is a Proposed Standard that obsoleted RFC 1884 and has itself been obsoleted by RFC 3513.

sections.title: The Addressing Model
sections.content:
IPv6 addresses are 128-bit identifiers for interfaces and sets of interfaces, and they are assigned to interfaces, not nodes. There are three types: unicast (one interface), anycast (a set of interfaces, delivered to the nearest one) and multicast (a set, delivered to all). There are no broadcast addresses, since multicast takes over their function.

Every interface must have at least one link-local unicast address, and may have several addresses of any type or scope. All zeros and all ones are legal values for any field unless specifically excluded.
sections.plainLanguage: An address names a door on a house, not the house. A door can have one name only it uses, a club name shared by many doors, or the name of the nearest of several matching doors.

sections.title: Writing Addresses and Prefixes
sections.content:
There are three conventional text forms. The preferred form is x:x:x:x:x:x:x:x, eight hexadecimal 16-bit pieces, where leading zeros in a field may be dropped. The :: form stands for one or more groups of zeros and may appear only once, so 1080:0:0:0:8:800:200C:417A can be written 1080::8:800:200C:417A. A mixed form, x:x:x:x:x:x:d.d.d.d, puts an IPv4 address in the low 32 bits, as in ::FFFF:129.144.52.38.

Prefixes use CIDR-like notation, ipv6-address/prefix-length, with the length in decimal. For example 12AB:0:0:CD30::/60 is a legal form of a 60-bit prefix, while dropping trailing zeros within a 16-bit chunk is not allowed.
sections.plainLanguage: Long addresses are written in eight chunks, and you can skip boring zeros. A double colon means 'a bunch of zeros are hiding here', but you can only use it once.

sections.title: Address Types and Unicast Forms
sections.content:
The type of an address is indicated by its leading bits, called the Format Prefix. Multicast addresses start with 1111 1111. Aggregatable global unicast uses 001, link-local 1111 1110 10, and site-local 1111 1110 11. The RFC says 15 percent of the address space is initially allocated and 85 percent is reserved for future use. Anycast addresses come from the unicast space and cannot be told apart by syntax.

Special unicast addresses: the unspecified address 0:0:0:0:0:0:0:0 (never assigned to a node, used as a source before an address is learned) and the loopback address 0:0:0:0:0:0:0:1 (a node sending to itself, never forwarded by a router). IPv4-compatible and IPv4-mapped addresses carry an IPv4 address in the low 32 bits, the second with FFFF before it.

For most prefixes from 001 to 111 (except multicast), interface identifiers must be 64 bits in EUI-64 format with the "u" bit inverted. Link-local addresses are for a single link and routers must not forward them to other links. Site-local addresses are for use inside a site and must not be forwarded outside it. The aggregatable global format is defined in RFC 2374.
sections.plainLanguage: The first few bits of an address say what kind it is, like the first letters of a postal code. Some addresses only work on your own street or in your own neighborhood, and routers will not carry them any farther.

sections.title: Anycast Addresses
sections.content:
An anycast address is a unicast-format address assigned to more than one interface, and a packet to it is routed to the nearest one by the routing protocols' measure of distance. Nodes must be explicitly configured to know an address is anycast. Because global anycast sets need a separate routing entry everywhere, support for them may be unavailable or very restricted.

Until more experience exists, two restrictions apply: an anycast address MUST NOT be used as the source of a packet, and it MUST NOT be assigned to a host, only to a router. The predefined Subnet-Router anycast address is the subnet prefix with the rest set to zero, and all routers are required to support it for the subnets they attach to.
sections.plainLanguage: Anycast is like calling 'the nearest pizza shop' of a chain: any one of them can answer, and you get whichever is closest.

sections.title: Multicast Addresses
sections.content:
A multicast address starts with 11111111, followed by 4 flag bits, a 4-bit scope and a 112-bit group ID. The three high flags are reserved and must be 0. The T flag is 0 for a permanently-assigned (well-known) group and 1 for a transient one. The scope limits how far the group reaches, from node-local (1) and link-local (2) to site-local (5), organization-local (8) and global (E).

The meaning of a permanent address does not depend on scope. The RFC's example is a group ID of 101 hex for NTP servers, so FF02:0:0:0:0:0:0:101 means all NTP servers on the same link. Multicast addresses must not be used as source addresses.

Predefined groups include All Nodes (FF01:0:0:0:0:0:0:1 and FF02:0:0:0:0:0:0:1) and All Routers (FF01, FF02 and FF05 with last group 2). The solicited-node address is formed by appending the low-order 24 bits of a unicast or anycast address to FF02:0:0:0:0:1:FF00::/104, and a node must join it for every such address it has.
sections.plainLanguage: A multicast address is a group chat. Part of the address says how far the message may travel: just this computer, this street, this site, or everywhere.

sections.title: A Node's Required Addresses
sections.content:
A host must recognize its link-local address for each interface, its assigned unicast addresses, the loopback address, the All-Nodes multicast addresses, the solicited-node address for each unicast and anycast address, and the other multicast groups it belongs to. A router must also recognize the Subnet-Router anycast addresses for its router interfaces, any other configured anycast addresses, and the All-Routers multicast addresses.

The security section is short: IPv6 addressing documents have no direct impact on Internet infrastructure security, and authentication of IPv6 packets is defined elsewhere. Appendix C lists the changes from RFC 1884, such as the new 001 prefix for aggregatable global unicast and a longer solicited-node prefix.
sections.plainLanguage: Every computer must answer to a standard list of names, such as its own, 'everyone', and its own loopback. Routers must also answer to a few extra names for their special job.

fields.name: flgs
fields.desc: Flags 0,0,0,T; T=1 marks a transient group.

fields.name: scop
fields.desc: Scope value limiting the reach of the group.

fields.name: group ID
fields.desc: Identifies the group within the scope.
